newsitem.title: GERMANY: Leica snaps back into profit.
newsitem.headline: Leica snaps back into profit.

text.p: Leica Camera AG Tuesday reported a return to profit in the first nine months of its fiscal year amid sharp productivity gains at its main plant.

The well known camera maker, which went public last year, said it had a net profit of 4.9 million marks ($3 million) in the nine months ended on Dec. 31 compared with a loss of 1.6 million marks ($980,000) in the year-earlier period.
Sales rose 7.1 percent to 174.8 million marks ($107 million).
A spokesman attributed the turnaround to investment in new machinery that had significantly shortened the time it takes to produce cameras, lenses and binoculars.

While many of Leica's cameras are as expensive as small cars, professional photographers account for just 10 percent of sales of its two top-of-the-range models, the M6 rangefinder camera and the R8 single-lens reflex.
"Most of our cameras are bought by ambitious amateurs who regard photography as their number one hobby," said Leica spokesman Hans Guenther von Zydowitz.

The manual focus R8, launched before Christmas and priced at 4,400 marks ($2,695) excluding a lens, is selling well and Leica plans to produce 5,000 to 6,000 of them by March 31, when its current fiscal year ends, von Zydowitz said.

Relying on demand from photography purists who insist on equipment that gives them complete creative control, Leica has avoided equipping its top models with automatic focusing and other features incorporated by competitors.
It also has no plans to follow rivals into the Advanced Photo System (APS) launched last year, a new generation of film and cameras that offers a range of picture formats from one film.
Von Zydowitz blamed the introduction of APS for unsettling prospective buyers and causing stagnation in the camera market last year.
Leica's compact camera subsidiary Minox, bought last April, should be running profitably by the end of the current fiscal year, Leica said.
